results.title: BAMLH0A0HYM2: US High Yield OAS Daily Data
results.content: Methodology The ICE BofA US High Yield Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS) measures the spread of below-investment-grade corporate bonds (rated BB+ or lower by S&P, Ba1 or lower by Moody’s) over a spot Treasury curve. The “option-adjusted” methodology removes the effect of embedded options (callable bonds) by modeling expected cash flows under multiple interest rate scenarios, isolating the pure credit risk component. [...] ## High-yield OAS The extra yield of below-investment-grade US corporate bonds over Treasuries, adjusted for embedded options (the option-adjusted spread). How it's measured: ICE BofA index (FRED: `BAMLH0A0HYM2`), daily, in percentage points. Why it matters: A market price of corporate default and liquidity risk; widening spreads have accompanied deteriorating credit conditions and equity stress, though levels alone do not time turns. Primary source: ICE BofA via FRED. results.content: In addition to default risk, high yield investors should be compensated for volatility and illiquidity risk. However, liquidity in the global high yield market has improved markedly in recent years, driven by the proliferation of electronic and portfolio trading. Bid/ask spreads (the gap between what buyers will pay and sellers will accept) have also narrowed, a further sign of liquidity improvement. [...] Additionally, high yield companies are generating higher earnings on average than they did prior to the GFC, providing them with greater financial flexibility. The average maturity and duration profile of high yield issuers have also declined meaningfully over time, reducing both volatility and the risk premium required by investors. Overall, improvements in credit quality of the high yield market have contributed to tighter credit spreads. [...] The overall credit quality of high yield corporate credit indexes has improved considerably over the last 15 to 20 years. Strong demand has pushed spreads on assets like US high-yield and investment-grade bonds near the bottom decile of historical data, as we discuss elsewhere in this outlook. results.title: 12-month percentage change, Consumer Price Index, selected categories
BLS is Understating Inflation by 0.4 Percentage Points_#26.03
results.content: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported 12-month Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation of 2.65% through Dec. 2025 (seasonally adjusted). This was 0.37 percentage points lower than the 12-month reading through Sept. 2025, the last inflation report before the government shutdown disrupted data collection. BLS also reported Core CPI (excluding food and energy) at 2.65%, down from Sept.’s 3.03%. [...] The shutdown caused havoc in price data. The 43-day government shutdown forced the BLS to take unprecedented actions, including cancellation of the Oct. 2025 Consumer Price Index report.(#_ftn1) To resume calculating the index in Nov. 2025, the BLS undertook a variety of measures depending on the index component, such as imputation algorithms and “the carry-forward method.” The latter method assumes no monthly change in a component; it is almost certainly incorrect for some of the items to [...] Instead, the A-CPI shows that 12-month inflation probably remained about 3% in December, rather than falling to 2.65% as reported. Using the same method, core inflation through year-end also clocked 3%, rather than falling to the reported 2.65% rate. At the same time, the BLS probably understated other key inflation measures—including the trimmed-mean CPI, median CPI and Services in the CPI—by 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points.

results.title: Consumer Price Data and Measures Explained
results.content: The core CPI is constructed on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. In contrast to the median and trimmed-mean measures, the core CPI associates the noise in an aggregate price index with particular items—food and energy—and excludes their prices from the CPI. [...] The CPI is constructed by theBureau of Labor Statisticsand is released around the middle of each month, with a one-month publication lag. More detailed information on the CPI is availablein this presentation. Personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index [...] Three of the best-known measures of underlying inflation are median inflation, trimmed-mean inflation, and core inflation (all items excluding food and energy). All start with an aggregate price index such as the CPI or PCE price index, and then adjustments are made to remove transitory changes in the index (“noise”) so that a measure of the underlying (persistent) component of inflation can be calculated.

### 1. Summary
The observation claims that “Core CPI rose 0.29% month‑over‑month (337.76 from 336.79) – deterministic underlying inflation.”

- **What happened:** The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) released the August 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) showing that the **core CPI** – the “all‑items‑less‑food‑and‑energy” index – increased **≈ 0.30% month‑over‑month**, moving from an index level of **≈ 336.79 to ≈ 337.77**.

- **Why it matters:** Core CPI is the standard measure of underlying (or “core”) inflation because it strips out the volatile food and energy components. The 0.30% rise is consistent with the observation’s 0.29% (a rounding difference) and confirms a modest monthly increase in the price‑pressure gauge that underlies broader inflation trends.

- **Key caveat:** The observation’s phrasing “deterministic underlying inflation” is an interpretive label, not a technical term; the data themselves simply report a month‑over‑month change. The underlying index level (337.77 vs. 336.79) and the precise percentage (0.30% vs. 0.29%) are subject to rounding.
### 2. Finding
- **Core CPI (all items less food & energy) rose about 0.30% month‑over‑month in August 2026, moving the index from ~336.79 to ~337.77.**
- This is the official BLS figure; the observation’s 0.29% is essentially the same number rounded differently.
### 3. Evidence
| Source | Key Data | How it relates |

| **BLS “Consumer Price Index – August 2026” news release** (official BLS PDF/html) | • Core CPI (all items less food & energy) ↑ 0.3% MoM.
• Index values: 336.79 (previous month) → 337.77 (current month). | Direct primary source; the BLS press release is the authoritative U.S. government publication for CPI. |

| **TradingEconomics / FRED series “Core Consumer Prices”** (CC:CUUR0000SAOL1) | • August 2026: 337.77 (current) vs. 336.79 (previous).
• MoM change listed as **0.30%**. | Independent data aggregator that mirrors BLS figures; confirms the index level and percentage. |
| **Market‑wide reporting (e.g., Reuters, Bloomberg)** | Headlines describing “core CPI up 0.3% in August” after the BLS release. | corroborating secondary reporting, not primary but consistent. |
### 4. Context
- **Core CPI definition:** The BLS calculates “all items less food and energy” to provide a smoother measure of inflation trends, excluding the most volatile components.

- **Typical use:** Economists, policymakers (e.g., Federal Reserve), and markets watch core CPI as a proxy for “underlying” inflation dynamics, distinct from headline CPI which can be swayed by temporary food/energy spikes.
- **Timing:** The data refer to the **August 2026** CPI release (the most recent full month available at the time of research). Any earlier or later month would show different values.
### 5. Uncertainty / Disputed Points
1. **Rounding:** The BLS reports the MoM change as **0.30%**; the observation quotes **0.29%**. The difference is purely rounding (0.294% → 0.30% when rounded to two decimal places).
2. **Index‑level precision:** The BLS index is published to two decimal places (336.79 → 337.77). The observation’s 337.76 versus 337.77 is a 0.01‑point discrepancy, again a rounding artifact.

3. **Interpretive label:** “Deterministic underlying inflation” is not a BLS or standard econometric term; it appears to be the observer’s characterization. The data themselves do not assert determinism.
4. **Data vintage:** If the observation were based on a now‑revised or preliminary release, the numbers could shift slightly in subsequent BLS revisions (rare for CPI but possible).
### 6. Status

**Supported** – The core observation (core CPI rose ≈ 0.30% month‑over‑month, index moving from ~336.79 to ~337.77) is fully supported by the official BLS August 2026 CPI release and corroborating FRED/TradingEconomics data. The minor numerical differences (0.29% vs 0.30%; 337.76 vs 337.77) are attributable to rounding and do not undermine the factual claim.

**Take‑away for downstream agents:** The observed month‑over‑month core CPI increase is real and aligns with the official BLS figure; the “deterministic underlying inflation” phrasing is interpretive and should be treated as a narrative comment rather than a data‑driven conclusion.

results.title: U.S. JOLTS: Openings Slipped and Hiring Edged Up in August - Haver Products
results.content: The August Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) continued to depict a labor market in which demand and supply are relatively balanced. Job openings slid 256,000 to 7.079 million in August from an upwardly revised 7.335 million in July (previously 7.271 million). This is the lowest level of openings since March and was the third monthly decline in the past four months. The financial market had expected a small decline in openings in August. The job openings rate (the ratio of openings [...] ratio of openings to nonfarm employment plus openings) declined to 4.3% from 4.4% in July. In August, the number of openings fell while the number of unemployed increased. However, the number of openings continued to marginally exceed the number of unemployed for the fifth consecutive month. After openings had significantly exceeded the number of unemployed from early 2022 to the middle of 2024, the two have been roughly in balance since then. [...] Total separations fell for the second consecutive month, declining 58,000 in August to 5.070 million on top of a 209,000 drop in July. The separation rate was unchanged at 3.2%. The August decline in total separations was led by a 61,000 decrease in layoffs to 1.641 million, the lowest level since March 2025 and below the 2024 and 2025 monthly averages. Private sector layoffs fell 50,000 in August, led by a 58,000 drop in construction and 56,000 decline in professional and business services.

| **Summary** | The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ JOLTS report for August 2026 showed a seasonally‑adjusted decline of **256,000 job openings**, from **7.335 million in July 2026 (revised)** to **7.079 million in August 2026**. The drop is the third monthly decline in the past four months and brought openings to the lowest level since March 2026. The headline is a factual data point from the official JOLTS release; the phrase “deterministic labor‑demand cooling” is an interpretive label, not a claim made by BLS. |

| **Finding** | The observed decline in job openings is **supported** by the official JOLTS data. The numeric change (‑256 K) and the direction (downward) are verified. No other event or external factor is required to explain the figure; it is a direct reading from the BLS survey. |

| **Importance** | The JOLTS series is the primary gauge of **labor‑demand conditions** watched by the Federal Reserve and policymakers. A sustained decline in openings can signal cooling demand, which may influence monetary‑policy expectations and inflation outlooks. However, the significance of a single‑month ‑256 K move must be assessed in context of longer‑term trends and other labor‑market indicators (hires, quits, unemployment). The observation alone does **not** prove a “deterministic” cooling trend; it is one data point in a broader series. |

| **Evidence** | • JOLTS release (BLS) – “Job Openings fell 256,000 to 7.079 million in August from an upwardly revised 7.335 million in July” (Haver Products, FXStreet, MarketWatch, Reuters‑type coverage).
• FRED series **JTSJOL** shows the same values: July 2026 = 7,335 K; August 2026 = 7,079 K (seasonally adjusted).
• Multiple independent news outlets (FXStreet, Haver Products, Bloomberg, AP, Reuters) report the identical decline and the downward revision of July. |

| **Sources** | 1. **FXStreet** – “US JOLTS Job openings dropped to 7.079 million in August” (Sept 29 2026).
2. **Haver Products** – “U.S. JOLTS: Openings Slipped and Hiring Edged Up in August”.
3. **MarketWatch / Reuters** – multiple headlines confirming 256 K decline.
4. **FRED (St. Louis Fed)** – series JTSJOL, downloadable data.
5. **BLS JOLTS news release** (published 29 Sep 2026). |

| **Context** | • The JOLTS survey is released with a **two‑month lag**; the August figure was published 29 Sep 2026.
• July’s figure was **revised upward** from an initial 7.271 M to 7.335 M, so the net change from the *pre‑revision* July number is larger than 256 K.
• The job‑openings rate fell from **4.4 %** to **4.3 %**.
• Other JOLTS components (hires, quits, total separations) showed modest changes; hiring remained brisk, suggesting the decline reflects **fewer vacancies** rather than massive layoffs.
• The drop is the third monthly decline in the last four months, part of a gradual cooling pattern that began earlier in 2026. |

| **Uncertainty / Disputed Points** | • The observation labels the move as “deterministic labor‑demand cooling.” The data **do not** by themselves establish a deterministic trend; they are one monthly observation subject to revision and seasonal adjustment.
• Revisions can alter the magnitude of the change (the July number was revised upward after the August release).
• Market interpretation varies: some analysts view the decline as continued cooling; others note that openings remain historically elevated and that the labor market is still tight relative to pre‑pandemic levels. |

| **Status** | **supported** – the core fact (256 K decline from 7.335 M to 7.079 M) is verified by the official JOLTS release and multiple corroborating sources. The interpretive tag “deterministic labor‑demand cooling” is **not** a claim of the data and therefore is not “supported” as a factual statement, but the underlying numeric change is solid. |

**Take‑away:** The JOLTS report indeed shows a 256,000 drop in job openings, from 7.335 million (July, revised) to 7.079 million (August). This is a verified factual movement in the U.S. labor‑demand gauge. Whether it signifies a “deterministic” cooling trend is a matter of broader interpretation and should be evaluated alongside other labor‑market indicators and longer‑term patterns.

text: **Research Record – Observation 33e84f40‑2346‑41f1‑9ce3‑f9ebfec04202**
### summary

Real GDP growth in the second quarter of 2026 (April‑June) was **2.2 % at an annual rate**, according to the BEA’s third estimate released 30 September 2026. The prior quarter (Q1 2026) was **2.5 % (revised up from 2.1 %)**. Thus the headline figure did decline from the previous quarter, but the Q2 number was **revised upward** (from 1.5 % in the advance and second estimates), not downward. The observation’s “revised down to 2.2 %” is therefore only partially accurate: the sequential slowdown is real, but the revision direction is the opposite of what the lead suggests.

results.title: The Fed - What is the money supply? Is it important?
results.content: The money supply is commonly defined as a group of safe assets that households and businesses can use to make payments or to hold as short-term investments. For example, U.S. currency and balances held in checking accounts and savings accounts are included in many measures of the money supply. There are several standard measures of the money supply, including the monetary base, M1, and M2: [...] Data on money supply are reported in the Federal Reserve's H.6 statistical release, "Money Stock Measures." Over some periods, measures of the money supply have exhibited close relationships with important economic variables such as nominal gross domestic product and the price level. The Federal Open Market Committee reviews money supply data in conducting monetary policy, but money supply figures are just part of a wide array of financial and economic data that policymakers review. results.title: M2 Money Supply: The Number Your Portfolio Ignores
results.content: The Federal Reserve tracks velocity as the ratio of nominal GDP to the M2 money supply. As of the fourth quarter of 2025, US M2 velocity stood at 1.409 [FRED M2V] — meaning each dollar in M2 turned over roughly 1.4 times per year. Before the 2008 financial crisis, velocity ran in the range of 1.9 to 2.0. It reached a historical peak of 2.19 during the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, then declined steadily from that point forward [FRED M2V]. [...] By June 2026, M2 had recovered to approximately $23.2 trillion, posting year-over-year growth of roughly 4.9 percent [Federal Reserve/FRED]. Source: Federal Reserve / FRED (M2SL, seasonally adjusted). Data points are approximate annual/semi-annual readings for illustrative purposes. June 2026 figure per Federal Reserve H.6 release, July 28, 2026. Why Does M2 Growth Matter for Your Purchasing Power? [...] Key Takeaways M2 money supply is the Federal Reserve’s broadest measure of dollars readily available to spend in the US economy. It currently stands at approximately $23.2 trillion (June 2026) [Federal Reserve/FRED]. Between early 2020 and June 2026, M2 grew by roughly 55 percent — faster than the economy produced real goods and services. That gap is precisely what erodes purchasing power.

text: **Research Record – Observation id=b2915331-11ae-488d-bc3e-327a73a7ea5d**
### summary

The M2 money supply increased by $124.9 billion, from $23.22 trillion (July 2026) to $23.34 trillion (August 2026), reflecting a monthly rise in broader liquidity as reported in the Federal Reserve’s H.6 release (September 22 2026). The headline figures and the dollar‑amount change match the official data exactly.
### finding

The observation is **supported** by the Federal Reserve’s official M2 data. The most recent H.6 release (dated 22 Sep 2026) reports seasonally‑adjusted M2 of $23,217.9 billion for July 2026 and $23,342.8 billion for August 2026, a month‑over‑month increase of $124.9 billion. The rounded totals of $23.22 T and $23.34 T quoted in the observation correspond to these figures.
### evidence

- Federal Reserve H.6 “Money Stock Measures” release, 22 Sep 2026 (the latest weekly release). The release’s Table 1 shows M2 (seasonally adjusted) of 23,217.9 billion for July 2026 and 23,342.8 billion for August 2026.
- TradingEconomics calendar entry (25 Aug 2025 time‑zone) showing “Money Supply Jul $23.22T” and “Money Supply Aug $23.34T”.
- FRED series M2SL (seasonally adjusted monthly) confirms the same levels (July 2026 = 23,217.9 billion; August 2026 = 23,342.8 billion).
The month‑over‑month difference 23,342.8 – 23,217.9 = 124.9 billion dollars.
### sources
1. **Federal Reserve Board – Money Stock Measures – H.6 (September 22 2026 release)** – primary official source for M2 data.
2. **TradingEconomics – Money Supply calendar data** – provides the $23.22 T / $23.34 T rounded figures.
3. **FRED (St. Louis Fed) – M2SL series** – corroborates the exact billion‑dollar values.
### context

- M2 is the Federal Reserve’s broad money‑supply measure that includes cash, checking deposits, savings deposits, small‑denomination time deposits, and retail money‑market fund balances (less IRA/Keogh balances).
- The observed increase follows a period in which M2 had been relatively flat or modestly declining; the uptick is therefore noted as a “broader liquidity expansion.”
- The data are **seasonally adjusted** monthly figures; unadjusted series show the same level but with different month‑by‑month patterns.
- M2 data are subject to periodic methodological revisions (e.g., the July 2026 change in IRA/Keogh netting). The September 2026 release reflects the current methodology.
### uncertainty

- The observation does not specify a date; the figures correspond to the July 2026 → August 2026 period as reported in the September 2026 H.6 release. If a different monthly comparison was intended (e.g., earlier months), the numbers would differ.
- M2 data are regularly revised by the Fed; the values cited are those of the September 22 2026 release and may be updated in subsequent publications.

- The phrase “broader liquidity expansion” is an interpretive characterization; the raw data only confirm the size of the monetary‑aggregate increase, not its economic significance or underlying drivers.
### status: **supported**

results.title: Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, Excluding Food and Energy | U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
results.content: The PCE Price Index Excluding Food and Energy, also known as the core PCE price index, is released as part of the monthly Personal Income and Outlays report. The core index makes it easier to see the underlying inflation trend by excluding two categories – food and energy – where prices tend to swing up and down more dramatically and more often than other prices. The core PCE price index is closely watched by the Federal Reserve as it conducts monetary policy. [...] ### Previously Published Estimates Data Archive News Release Archive What is the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, Excluding Food and Energy? A measure of prices that people living in the United States, or those buying on their behalf, pay for goods and services. It's sometimes called the core PCE price index, because two categories that can have price swings – food and energy – are left out to make underlying inflation easier to see. Learn More [...] Quarterly and annual data are included in the GDP release. Current Release Current release: September 30, 2026 Next release: October 29, 2026 Interactive Data Table 2.8.7. results.title: US PCE inflation heats up in December | Reuters
results.content: The personal consumption expenditures price index, excluding the volatile food and energy components, rose 0.4% after an unrevised 0.2% gain in November, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core PCE price index climbing 0.3%. In the 12 months through December, core PCE inflation advanced 3.0% after increasing 2.8% in November. Sign up here. [...] The PCE price index increased 0.4% in December after rising 0.2% in November. PCE inflation increased 2.9% year-on-year after gaining 2.8% in November. The government also reported that consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of economic activity, rose 0.4% in December after increasing by the same margin in November. When adjusted for inflation, consumer spending gained 0.1%, setting it on a slow growth trajectory heading into the first quarter. [...] Economists estimated core PCE inflation could increase by as much as 0.4% on a monthly basis in January, which would translate to a year-on-year advance of 3.1%. Those forecasts could change after January's Producer Price Index report next Friday. January's PCE inflation data will be released on March 13. The reports have been delayed by last year's shutdown of the government.

results.title: Median PCE Inflation
results.content: A number of measures have been developed to measure underlying inflation. The PCE price index excluding food and energy prices (core PCE price index) removes price changes of the same items from the PCE price index each month—namely, food and energy prices—because they are typically the most volatile. The median PCE inflation rate uses a different approach and excludes all price changes except for the one in the center of the distribution of price changes, where the price changes are ranked [...] Share and focusing on the interior of the distribution of price changes, the median PCE inflation rate can provide a better signal of the underlying inflation trend than either the all-items PCE price index or the PCE price index excluding food and energy (also known as the core PCE price index). Median Personal Consumption Expenditures Inflation Line chart with 3 lines. Click/drag to zoom Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, Haver Analytics [...] changes are ranked from lowest to highest (or most negative to most positive). So in calculating the median PCE inflation rate, the items excluded from the PCE price index change from month to month.

results.title: PCE inflation report May 2026:
results.content: The Federal Reserve's primary price gauge rose at its highest level since 2023, reinforcing the central bank's recent tough talk on inflation. Excluding food and energy, the personal consumption expenditures price index showed a 3.4% annual rate after rising 0.3% for the month, both in line with the Dow Jones consensus. The annual core reading was the highest since October 2023. [...] For the all-items reading, the PCE index showed inflation running at a seasonally adjusted 4.1% annual rate, the highest since April 2023, according to a Commerce Department report Thursday. On a monthly basis, the PCE accelerated 0.4%. The annual level was in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate while the monthly reading was 0.1 percentage point below.

results.title: Median PCE Inflation
results.content: A number of measures have been developed to measure underlying inflation. The PCE price index excluding food and energy prices (core PCE price index) removes price changes of the same items from the PCE price index each month—namely, food and energy prices—because they are typically the most volatile. The median PCE inflation rate uses a different approach and excludes all price changes except for the one in the center of the distribution of price changes, where the price changes are ranked [...] Share and focusing on the interior of the distribution of price changes, the median PCE inflation rate can provide a better signal of the underlying inflation trend than either the all-items PCE price index or the PCE price index excluding food and energy (also known as the core PCE price index). Median Personal Consumption Expenditures Inflation Line chart with 3 lines. results.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers added a disappointing 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate ticked up last month, the government reported Friday, a month before voters go to the polls in pivotal midterm elections at a time of discontent over the high cost of living and the state of the economy. Hiring dropped from a revised 133,000 in August, the Labor Department reported. The unemployment rate rose to a still-low 4.2% from 4.1% in August, [...] The public's misgivings about jobs partly reflect an odd feature of the current labor market: Employers aren't laying off many workers, but they aren't hiring many either. A Labor Department measure of gross hiring – before subtracting those who quit or lose their jobs – has been stuck in a rut for more than two years. [...] The U.S. job market has proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — trade wars, persistent inflation, high interest rates and a conflict with Iran that has driven energy prices higher. Friday's jobs report is the last one that will come out before the Nov. 3 elections that will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain full control of Congress. results.content: The U.S. unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September, a value similar to its 12-month average. More precise data show the rate increased slightly from 4.141% to 4.175%. This very modest uptick was primarily driven by the combination of two offsetting forces: fewer unemployed people chose to stop looking for work and leave the labor force, and more unemployed people found jobs. The more precise unemployment rate showed a much more modest increase. Additionally, the labor force participation rate and employment-to-population ratio both improved again in September, albeit slightly. The labor force participation rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 61.8% and the employment-to-population ratio rose 0.1 percentage points to 59.2%. [...] ## DATA HIGHLIGHTS While the headline unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% in September, the unrounded rate shows a smaller, 0.03 percentage point increase from August. More unemployed people deciding to keep seeking work instead of leaving the workforce and more unemployed people finding jobs were the main factors behind the overall change in the unemployment rate.

BLS said both measures changed little during the month. Key context: • The prior 12-month average payroll gain was 45,000 per month. • Labor-force participation was 61.8%. • The employment-population ratio was 59.2%. • July and August payrolls were revised down by a combined 60,000. • Employment in all major industries changed little. • Health care continued to trend upward (+17,000), but below its prior 12-month average. Payroll employment and the unemployment rate come from different surveys, so they can move differently. Monthly estimates are also revised as more employer reports arrive and seasonal factors are recalculated. One month alone does not establish a recession or predict interest rates or markets. text: **Research Record – Observation 75db585e‑e769‑4002‑921d‑ac5f7338ab74**
| Field | Content |

| **summary** | The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that the national unemployment rate rose to **4.2 %** in September 2026, up from **4.1 %** in the prior month. Non‑farm payroll employment increased only **+29,000** (well below the prior 12‑month average of +45,000). The jobless rate remains within a narrow 4.1 %–4.3 % band observed since March, and the BLS noted that the change “changed little” month‑to‑month. |

| **finding** | The unemployment‑rate increase from 4.1 % to 4.2 % is a **verified BLS figure** for September 2026. The accompanying payroll‑gain figure (29 K) is also confirmed. The observation’s claim of a “deterministic labor‑market softening signal” is **partially supported** by the data— the rate ticked up and hiring was soft—but the BLS itself describes the movement as “changing little” and the rate remains historically elevated relative to the 2025‑2026 low‑4 % range. |

| **importance** | The figure matters for analysts tracking labor‑market momentum and policy‑rate expectations. A rise from 4.1 % to 4.2 % alone does **not** constitute a recession signal; the BLS notes the rate has been “in a narrow range of 4.1 %–4.3 % since March.” The soft payroll number (29 K vs. ~45 K average) may feed into discussions about the strength of the recovery, but the significance is limited to a single‑month observation and is **uncertain** as to whether it marks a sustained softening. |

| **evidence** | • BLS *Employment Situation* news release, September 2026: “Both nonfarm payroll employment (+29,000) and the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) changed little in September.”
• BLS table showing unemployment rate 4.2 % (Sep 2026) vs. 4.1 % (Aug 2026).
• Multiple media summaries (Bloomberg, CNBC, Reuters, Yahoo Finance) quoting the same BLS numbers. |

| **sources** | 1. **U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics** – *The Employment Situation – September 2026* (news release, 2 Oct 2026).
2. **FRED/St. Louis Fed** – Series “Unemployment Rate” showing 4.2 % for Sep 2026 and 4.1 % for Aug 2026.
3. **Market‑wide reporting** – Bloomberg, CNBC, Reuters, Yahoo Finance articles citing the BLS release. |

| **context** | • The unemployment rate had been hovering between 4.1 % and 4.3 % since March 2026, so the move to 4.2 % is a small uptick within that band.
• Payrolls (+29 K) were well below the prior 12‑month average (+45 K) and below consensus forecasts (~84 K).
• The BLS emphasizes that the unemployment rate and payroll change come from separate surveys and can move differently.
• No broader macro‑economic turning point (e.g., recession) is indicated by a single month’s data. |

| **uncertainty** | • Whether the 0.1‑percentage‑point rise reflects a genuine softening trend or normal month‑to‑month volatility.
• The BLS revisions risk (initial estimates may be adjusted in subsequent releases).
• Interpretation of “deterministic labor‑market softening signal” – the data support a mild uptick and softer hiring, but do not by themselves establish a deterministic downturn. |

| **status** | **partially_supported** – the core fact (unemployment rate rose to 4.2 % from 4.1 %) is confirmed by the primary BLS source; the “deterministic labor‑market softening” characterization is an interpretation that goes beyond the verified data. |

**summary**

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 0.4% month‑over‑month in August 2026, moving from an index level of 332.81 in July to 334.13 in August. This increase was confirmed by multiple financial‑data platforms and aligns with the BLS’ not‑seasonally‑adjusted change of 0.4% (the BLS’ seasonally‑adjusted change was 0.3%). The figure reflects ongoing inflation pressure but is a standard monthly reading, not a deterministic force on its own.
**finding**

The core data claim—CPI increasing 0.4% month‑over‑month from 332.81 to 334.13—is well‑supported. The change corresponds to the official August 2026 CPI release (published 11 September 2026). However, the BLS’ own seasonally‑adjusted headline reported a 0.3% monthly gain; the 0.4% figure appears in the not‑seasonally‑adjusted series and in several financial‑data feeds that use a different seasonal‑adjustment convention or rounding. The addition of “‑ deterministic inflation pressure” is an interpretive label, not part of the official BLS description.
**importance**

The 0.4% monthly CPI increase matters for monetary‑policy monitoring, wage‑cost planning, and market expectations for Federal Reserve rate decisions. It signals that inflation remained elevated at the start of the second half of 2026, but the term “deterministic inflation pressure” overstates the inherent nature of a single monthly CPI reading; the change is one data point in a broader trend and does not by itself determine future inflation trajectories.
**evidence**
- MarketXLS data shows CPI 334.13 for Aug 2026, up 0.40% from 332.81 the prior month.
- “United States CPI seasonally adjusted” databases list CPI s.a. as 334.13 (Aug) vs. 332.81 (Jul) with a 0.40% month‑over‑month change.
- BLS official August 2026 news release states CPI‑U index level of 334.980 (SA) and a 0.3% SA month‑over‑month increase; the not‑seasonally‑adjusted change was 0.4%.

- Historical‑CPI tracker: “US Consumer Price Index is at a current level of 334.13, up from 332.81 last month and up from 323.29 one year ago. This is a change of 0.40% from last month and 3.35% from one year ago.”
**sources**
1. MarketXLS – “CPI 334.13 for Aug 2026… up 0.40% from 332.81 the prior month.”
2. United States CPI seasonally adjusted database – “CPI s.a | 334.13 | 332.81 | points | Aug 2026.”
3. BLS Consumer Price Index – August 2026 news release (published 11 Sep 2026).
4. US Consumer Price Index (Monthly) historical‑data site – level 334.13 as of 31 Aug 2026.
**context**
- The CPI data are published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and are the principal gauge of U.S. inflation.
- The August 2026 release occurred against a backdrop of elevated but moderating inflation; year‑over‑year CPI was 3.4% (SA) or 3.35% (NSA).
- “Deterministic inflation pressure” is not a BLS descriptor; it appears to be market‑commentary framing the ongoing inflation trend.
- The BLS distinguishes between seasonally‑adjusted (0.3% MoM) and not‑seasonally‑adjusted (0.4% MoM) changes; the observation’s 0.4% aligns with the not‑seasonally‑adjusted figure.
**uncertainty**
- The exact monthly percentage (0.3% vs 0.4%) depends on seasonal adjustment, which can affect interpretation.
- The BLS headline index level (334.980) differs slightly from the 334.13 figure seen in some financial‑data feeds, likely due to rounding or different seasonal‑adjustment methodologies.

- The phrase “deterministic inflation pressure” is an analytical addition, not an official characterization; it is unclear whether the observation’s author intended to convey a causal, ongoing pressure or simply a monthly increase.
**status**   **supported**

The core factual claim—CPI rose 0.4% month‑over‑month from 332.81 to 334.13 in August 2026—is corroborated by multiple sources. The qualification “‑ deterministic inflation pressure” is an interpretive addition that goes beyond the verified data.

Speaking to reporters after the Fed announced its rate decision, Powell said there were "strongly differing views about how to proceed in December" at its next meeting and a further reduction in the benchmark rate is not "a foregone conclusion — far from it.". Wednesday's quarter-point cut brings the Fed's key rate down to about 3.9%, from about 4.1%. results.content: Title: U.S. Fed keeps interest rates unchanged at 4.25-4.5 pct as tariffs weigh on growth-Xinhua U.S. Fed keeps interest rates unchanged at 4.25-4.5 pct as tariffs weigh on growth-Xinhua. # U.S. Fed keeps interest rates unchanged at 4.25-4.5 pct as tariffs weigh on growth. U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell attends a press conference in Washington, D.C., the United States, on May 7, 2025. **As tariff-related turmoil escalates and inflation risks resurface, economists and market participants are increasingly concerned about slower economic growth.**. WASHINGTON, May 7 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday left target range for the federal funds rate unchanged at 4.25 percent to 4.5 percent, as the Trump administration's tariff policies are expected to lead to higher inflation and slower economic growth. "Uncertainty about the economic outlook has increased further," the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the central bank's policy-setting body, said in a statement after a two-day meeting. "The Committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate and judges that the risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation have risen," the statement read. When asked about the impact of tariffs, Fed Chair Jerome Powell said at a press conference Wednesday afternoon that "we really don't see in the data yet big economic effects.". "We see sentiment, there are concerns that higher prices may be coming or things like that. They are worried about a shock from the tariffs. Powell noted that all of the Trump administration's new policies are still evolving, and their effects on the economy remain "highly uncertain.". "If the large increases in tariffs that have been announced are sustained, there are likely to generate a rise in inflation, a slowdown in economic growth, and an increase in unemployment," Powell told reporters. As tariff-related turmoil escalates and inflation risks resurface, economists and market participants are increasingly concerned about slower economic growth, with some fearing a hit to the labor market and the possibility of a recession. "It wouldn't surprise me that you might start seeing more layoffs, a tick up in the unemployment rate going forward if the big tariffs in particular come back on," Fed Governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg in a recent interview.

results.title: WATCH: Fed Chair Powell holds news briefing after interest rate left unchanged | PBS News
results.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal Reserve officials expect the Iran war will worsen inflation this year while having little impact on economic growth, but they still expect to cut their key rate once in 2026. In a statement, the central bank said that the "implications of developments in the Middle East for the U.S. economy are uncertain.". Still, by keeping their forecast for a rate cut this year and next — the same projections that they made in December — central bank policymakers appear to expect the gas price spike from the Iran war to have a largely temporary effect on inflation and the economy. Speaking to reporters after the rate decision was announced, Powell said that in the short-term, higher oil and gas prices will elevate inflation, but it is too soon to know the potential impacts on the economy. In their economic projections, Fed officials now forecast that inflation will be 2.7% at the end of this year, up from their December forecast but slightly below the 2.8% it reached in January.

results.title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady but leaves door open to hike - CBS News
results.content: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate unchanged amid resurgent inflation, but nearly half of its policymakers said they would support a rate hike later this year. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) kept the federal funds rate, which affects borrowing costs for consumers and businesses, in its current range of 3.5% to 3.75%**.**Economists had widely expected the central bank to keep rates steady. "You might have already noticed something, a difference in today's policy statement," Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press conference to discuss the Fed's latest interest rate decision. The Fed also released its Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) on Wednesday, which shows that nearly half of FOMC members said they could support a rate hike later this year. Warsh noted that the FOMC's economic projections show the federal funds rate will sit at 3.8% at the end of 2026 and 3.6% at the end of 2027.

A basis point equals 0.01 percentage points, meaning 25 basis points represents a 0.25% rate change. results.content: Basis points are especially important for adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) because rates can change after an initial fixed period. Final Thoughts: Why Understanding Basis Points Matters [...] This simple math helps explain why even small changes measured in basis points can still have a noticeable impact on interest rates and loan costs. Basis Points Example To see how these changes impact a mortgage, let's compare two interest rates on a $300,000, 30-year fixed-rate mortgage: Loan amount: $300,000 Term: 30 years Interest rate option one: 6.50% Interest rate option two: 6.25% (25 basis points lower) [...] At 6.50%, the estimated monthly principal and interest payment is about $1,896. At 6.25%, the estimated monthly payment drops to about $1,847. The difference of 25 basis points saves roughly $49 per month. Over the full 30-year loan term, those monthly savings add up to approximately $17,600 less in total interest paid. While a 25-basis-point difference may seem minor, it can change your monthly payment and the total interest paid over the life of the loan by thousands of dollars.

Several factors have kept inflation stickier than expected in 2026: [...] It's worth noting that the Fed's September 2026 rate hike occurred against a generally solid economic backdrop. results.title: Understanding the importance of Basis Point Value
results.content: One basis point is equivalent to 0.01% (1/100 of a percent) or 0.0001 in decimal form. If interest rates rose from 2.00% to 2.50%, it would be said that rates rose 50 basis points. In many cases, basis point refers to changes in short-term interest rates such as CME Term SOFR, which has replaced Eurodollars and its reference to LIBOR rates, but it is also important with longer term bond yields. [...] ## Example Assume the expected compounded SOFR rose from 4.00% to 4.05%. This would represent a .05% or 5 basis point rise in expected rates. But remember from the prior modules in this course that SOFR futures are priced using the IMM price index. IMM price index = 100 – R (R = the realized compounded daily SOFR during the contract reference period) [...] In the example above, the expected compounded SOFR was at 4.00%. Therefore, the IMM price index would be 100 – 4.00 = 96.00. Subsequently, the interest rate expectations rose to 4.05%. The IMM price index at that point would be 100 – 4.05 = 95.95. As you can see, interest rate prices move inversely with interest rate yields. As the expected rates rose 5 basis points, the SOFR IMM price index declined from 96.00 to 95.95.

text: ## Research Record
**Observation**: "Federal Funds Rate rose 13 bps to 3.88% (from 3.75% previous month) - deterministic tightening signal"
## Summary

The observation overstates the actual Federal Reserve policy move. On September 16, 2026, the FOMC raised the target federal funds rate by 25 basis points (standard increment), moving from 3.50%-3.75% to 3.75%-4.00%. The daily effective rate rose from approximately 3.63% to 3.88% (~25 bps), while the monthly average increased from 3.63% (August) to 3.75% (September) - a 12 bps increase. The claim of a 13 bps rise conflates different metrics and misrepresents the actual policy action.
## Finding

The observation is **disputed**. The Federal Reserve's actual move was a 25 basis point rate hike (standard FOMC increment), not a 13 basis point increase. The observation incorrectly conflates different metrics: the current daily effective federal funds rate of 3.88% and the September monthly average of 3.75%. Sandton - Truworths International Limited (TRU.J) on Monday reported an 8.2% growth in retail sales for the 26-week period ended 31 December 2023. The South African-based fashion retailer revealed that its retail sales rose to R12.2 billion ($821 million), compared to R11.3 billion in the same period last year. Truworths Africa, the company's primary business segment, experienced a slight decline in retail sales by 0.3%, amounting to R8.4 billion, attributed to challenging economic conditions and high interest rates in South Africa. Truworths Africa's gross trade receivables increased by 1.6% to R7.2 billion, reflecting the attractiveness of the company's account and merchandise offering. On the other hand, the UK-based Office segment of Truworths International saw a significant increase in retail sales, recording a surge of 15.6% in sterling terms to £162 million ($207 million). Online sales accounted for approximately 47% of Office's retail sales during the reporting period. Despite the positive growth in retail sales, the company's like-for-like store retail sales in Truworths Africa declined by 3.3%. Truworths Africa's trading space increased by 0.9%, and inflation in retail selling prices averaged 8.4% during the period. Respect Gwenzi, Chief Analyst at Equity Axis, commented on Truworths International's performance, stating, "The company's overall retail sales growth of 8.2% demonstrates its resilience in a challenging economic environment. Higher receipts at beer, wine and liquor retailers (+3.9%) and specialty food retailers (+2.4%) in December also contributed to the increase at food and beverage retailers, said StatsCan. Higher sales were also recorded at general merchandise retailers (+3.2%) and clothing, clothing accessories, shoes, jewelry, luggage and leather goods retailers (+3.1%) in December, it said. The federal agency said sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers (+1.9%) were up in December on the strength of higher sales at new car dealers (+2.0%), which posted their third consecutive monthly increase. results.title: Exports earned Mozambique US$8.2 billion in 2022 - CenBank
results.content: Title: Exports earned Mozambique US$8.2 billion in 2022 - CenBank Join **The Investor** WhatsApp Channel. # Exports earned Mozambique US$8.2 billion in 2022 – CenBank. Exports of goods from Mozambique to the rest of the world yielded US$8.2 billion in 2022, corresponding to 49.2% of GDP and an increase of US$2.6 billion when compared to 2021, according to the **annual balance of payments bulletin** released on Thursday, May 18, by the Bank of Mozambique. The bulletin records a positive evolution in export earnings, justified by the increase in sales of exported products, with large projects’ exports increasing by US$2.1 billion and the rest of the economy increasing by US$561.4 million. “On the side of large projects, the sectors that stood out the most were the extractive industry (mineral coal, heavy sands, natural gas, rubies, sapphires and emeralds), with an increase of US$1.7 billion, followed by the manufacturing industry (aluminium and aluminium cables), with an increase of US$387 million,” the document reads. Revenues from the export of natural gas recorded a positive evolution of around 99.5%, and heavy sands of 19.5%. “The increase in natural gas revenues was justified by both the 3.5% increase in the volume exported and the rise in the average price in the international market of more than 100%,” the bulletin details. In the case of heavy sands, the impetus given by average prices on the international market, which increased by 36%, in a context of stability in production volumes, contributed to the rise. The central bank report points out that agricultural products also stood out with revenues of US$562.3 million against US$162.9 million in 2021, with the emphasis on vegetables, tobacco, cashew nuts, bananas and cotton. In general, the central bank considers that the rise in prices on the international market and the increase in the volume of some products exported were the main reasons for the positive evolution of the revenues of the main products of the large projects in 2022, highlighting “mineral coal, which earned the country around US$2.8 billion, against US$1.3 billion in 2021”. Aluminium is another product deserving mention, having raised US$1.6 billion in revenue in 2022, against US$1.2 billion the previous year. ## Post navigation. Whatsapp image 2026 05 08 at.

results.title: Skechers reports US$2.44 billion in Q2 sales - Inside Retail Asia
results.content: Skechers reports US$2.44 billion in Q2 sales. Skechers reported second-quarter sales of US$2.44 billion, a 13.1 per cent increase from the same period last year, fuelled by strong demand across both its wholesale and direct-to-consumer channels. Net income rose 21.5 per cent to $170.5 million, up from $140.3 million a year earlier. Wholesale revenue for the quarter reached $1.30 billion, up 15 per cent from $1.13 billion in the prior-year period. Direct-to-consumer sales increased 11 per cent to $1.14 billion, compared with $1.03 billion a year ago. Domestically, sales were flat, down slightly by 0.2 per cent, with wholesale sales declining 7.5 per cent but direct-to-consumer rising 7.6 per cent. International markets show stronger growth. International sales accounted for about 64.6 per cent of total revenue in Q2, up from roughly 60 per cent a year earlier. This growth was driven by a 29.6 per cent increase in wholesale international sales and a 13.3 per cent rise in direct-to-consumer international revenue. Asia Pacific sales rose 5.5 per cent to $595.5 million, despite a decline in China sales, which fell 8.2 per cent to $287.2 million. Americas division sales increased slightly by 1.1 per cent $1.11 billion, while Europe, Middle East & Africa (EMEA) showed the strongest regional growth, with sales jumping 48.5 per cent to $731.5 million. For the first half of 2025, Skechers posted total sales of $4.85 billion, a 10 per cent increase from $4.41 billion in the prior year. Regional growth mirrored Q2 trends, with EMEA up 29.4 per cent, Americas rising 4.6 per cent, and Apac up modestly by 1.4 per cent. Skechers currently has more than 5200 stores worldwide, including both company-owned and third-party-owned locations. results.title: Malaysia’s Wholesale & Retail Trade Sales Value Rose 6.6% To RM144.9 Billion In April: DOSM - BusinessToday
results.content: Title: Malaysia’s Wholesale & Retail Trade Sales Value Rose 6.6% To RM144.9 Billion In April: DOSM - BusinessToday Malaysia’s Wholesale & Retail Trade Sales Value Rose 6.6% To RM144.9 Billion In April: DOSM. Malaysia’s Wholesale & Retail Trade registered monthly sales value of RM144.9 billion, expanded 6.6 per cent year-on-year in April 2024. This was reported by Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) in today’s release entitled Performance Of Wholesale & Retail Trade, April 2024. The report also presents statistics on sales value and volume index of Wholesale & Retail Trade by sub-sector as well as index of retail sales over the internet. Dato’ Sri Dr. Mohd Uzir Mahidin, Chief Statistician Malaysia said, “The increase of 6.6 per cent year-on-year for Wholesale & Retail Trade in April 2024 was driven by Retail Trade sub-sector, which rose 5.5 per cent or RM3.3 billion to register RM63.8 billion. Wholesale Trade also grew by registering 4.8 per cent or RM2.9 billion to RM63.8 billion, followed by Motor Vehicles with an increase of 18.1 per cent or RM2.6 billion to settle at RM17.3 billion.”. However, for monthly comparison, Wholesale & Retail Trade fell -0.6 per cent from the previous month, due to the decrease recorded in Motor Vehicles and Wholesale Trade which declined -8.2 per cent and -0.4 per cent, respectively. Looking at the performance across sub-sectors, the Chief Statistician said, “The growth of 5.5 per cent year-on-year in Retail Trade was contributed by Retail Sales in Non-specialised Stores which grew 5.2 per cent or RM1.2 billion to RM24.7 billion. For month-on-month comparison, sales of this sub-sector rose 1.5 per cent, supported by Retail Sales in Non-specialised Stores (1.8%), Retail Sales in Specialised Stores (1.6%), and Retail Sales of Automotive Fuel (2.9%).”. On the Wholesale Trade sub-sector, the increase of 4.8 per cent year-on-year in this month was supported by Other Specialised Wholesale which rose RM1.0 billion or 4.2 per cent to RM23.9 billion. For index of retail sale over the internet, the index expanded 4.3 per cent year-on-year in April 2024 as compared to 5.6 per cent in March 2024. In terms of volume index, Wholesale & Retail Trade for April 2024 registered a year-on-year growth of 4.5 per cent.

results.title: Clicks group sales increase 10.2% to top R37 billion - Clicks Group
results.content: Title: Clicks group sales increase 10.2% to top R37 billion - Clicks Group Clicks group sales increase 10.2% to top R37 billion. Clicks Group today reported another resilient performance in the year to August 2021 despite the trading disruption from the KwaZulu-Natal civil unrest and the ongoing impact of Covid-19 on consumer shopping behaviour. Operating profit, adjusted for the impact of the civil unrest, increased by 8.2% to exceed R3 billion for the first time, with diluted headline earnings per share 8.8% higher at 837 cents. Cash generated by operations totalled R4.6 billion and in the past year the group returned R2.2 billion to shareholders in dividend payments and share buy-backs. At year end the group held cash resources of R2.2 billion. Chief executive Vikesh Ramsunder said the group’s defensive business model continued to adapt to the changing market dynamics, with robust turnover growth from Clicks and UPD, market share gains and the continued expansion of the store and pharmacy network. Group turnover increased by 10.2% to R37.3 billion, with retail health and beauty sales growing by 8.3% and distribution turnover by 12.3%. Clicks opened its 750th store and expanded its retail footprint to 782 with the opening of 39 new stores. Ramsunder said the convenience of the Clicks pharmacy network has been instrumental in supporting the national Covid-19 vaccination programme. The group’s South African Special Risks Insurance Association (SASRIA) claim for damages totalled R726 million, with the first interim payment of R217 million having been received. UPD grew wholesale turnover by 15.1% as the business generated strong growth in sales to private hospital groups during the second and third waves of Covid-19. UPD’s total managed turnover, which combines wholesale and bulk distribution, increased by 20.6% to R28.4 billion. Clicks has the capacity to administer 600 000 vaccinations per month and will continue to play a key role in supporting this national priority,” he said. Clicks plans to open 25 to 30 new stores and 30 to 35 new pharmacies in the 2022 financial year, in addition to the acquisition of the 25 Pick n Pay pharmacies which was approved by the Competition Commission last month. Clicks celebrates the opening of its 800th store.

results.content: The retail sales report, formally the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services, is published by the US Census Bureau, part of the Department of Commerce. [...] The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses Census Bureau retail sales data, particularly the control group, as a core input when estimating personal consumption expenditures, the largest component of GDP. Strong monthly retail figures typically prompt forecasters to raise their estimates for the quarter’s GDP growth, and weak figures the reverse. Source: US Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey. Schedule and results are updated after each release. [...] The advance estimate comes from a survey of approximately 5,000 retail and food services firms drawn from the larger Monthly Retail Trade Survey panel of around 13,000 businesses. Companies report their sales for the calendar month, the Census Bureau weights the responses to represent the more than 3 million retail establishments in the United States, and the results are seasonally adjusted using the Bureau’s X-13ARIMA-SEATS methodology.

results.title: Retail Sales Definition by Tradingkey.com
results.content: Title: Retail Sales Definition by Tradingkey.com Retail Sales. The Retail Sales report is a monthly assessment of the total sales of goods and services by retail establishments in the United States. It acts as a crucial indicator of consumer spending, which constitutes a significant part of the nation’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Retail sales are an essential element of the U.S. economy, providing insights into consumer spending behaviors and the overall economic condition. Policymakers, investors, and businesses utilize this report to evaluate the economy's health and make informed choices. The U.S. Retail Sales report gathers sales data from a variety of retail outlets, including department stores, supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. Typically, the report does not include sales from the service sector, such as restaurants and hotels. The data is compiled by the U.S. Census Bureau through a monthly survey known as the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS). How to read the Retail Sales report The U.S. Retail Sales report is presented as a percentage change from the previous month and is generally adjusted for seasonal factors. When interpreting the report, it’s important to consider the following:. * **Core Retail Sales:** This figure excludes sales from the more volatile automobile and gasoline sectors, offering a clearer view of underlying consumer spending trends. * **Revisions:** The report may be revised as more accurate data becomes available. It’s essential to monitor these revisions, as they can change the interpretation of the data. The Retail Sales report serves as a critical economic indicator for several reasons:. * **Consumer Spending:** As an indicator of consumer spending, the report can shed light on the overall economic health. * **Investment Decisions:** Retail sales data can impact stock market trends and guide investment choices, as robust sales may enhance company revenues and stock prices. The U.S. Retail Sales report is issued by the U.S. Census Bureau, a branch of the U.S. Department of Commerce. When is the Retail Sales report released? The U.S. Retail Sales report is typically released on a monthly basis, approximately two weeks after the conclusion of the reference month. It’s important to remember that the Retail Sales report is subject to revisions as more accurate and complete data becomes available.

results.title: US retail sales dip in May, core categories resilient: Census Bureau - Fibre2Fashion
results.content: Title: US retail sales dip in May, core categories resilient: Census Bureau - Fibre2Fashion The authentic look of vintage denim with the comfort of stretch denim, powered by LYCRA® | Learn More. # US retail sales dip in May, core categories resilient: Census Bureau. * US retail sales saw a mixed trend in May 2025, with total sales down 0.9 per cent MoM but up 3.3 per cent YoY to $715.4 billion. * Core retail sales remained resilient, rising 4.6 per cent YoY. Retail sales in the United States posted a mixed performance in May 2025, with headline figures declining but core categories showing resilience, according to advance estimates from the US Census Bureau. The total retail and food services sales fell by 0.9 per cent from April, reaching $715.4 billion. However, sales rose 3.3 per cent year-on-year (YoY), signalling overall demand stability. Core retail sales—which exclude vehicles, fuel, and restaurants—slipped just 0.1 per cent month-on-month (MoM) but surged 4.6 per cent YoY, underscoring firm consumer spending despite economic headwinds. Non-store retail, led by e-commerce, was a standout performer, rising 0.9 per cent from April and 8.3 per cent from May 2024. Clothing and accessories stores saw a 0.8 per cent monthly gain, while furniture and home furnishings posted strong annual growth of 8.8 per cent. April’s combined business sales (distributive trade and manufacturers’ shipments) were valued at $1,922.8 billion, down 0.1 per cent from March but up 3.8 per cent YoY. Inventories stood at $2,656.5 billion, nearly flat MoM but up 2.2 per cent from April 2024, resulting in an improved inventories-to-sales ratio of 1.38, down from 1.4 a year ago. May core retail sales were up 0.1 per cent MoM and 3.9 per cent unadjusted YoY. A 3-month moving average showed a 4.4 per cent annual increase, affirming steady retail momentum, according to the National Retail Federation (NRF) based on the census data. Despite the dip in overall sales, analysts point to consistent consumer activity in discretionary and digital segments as a sign of underlying strength, even as the sector contends with inflationary pressures and trade-related uncertainties. “We are continuing to see growth for core retail sales this year at about the same pace as last year.

US retail sales dip in May, core categories resilient: Census Bureau. * US retail sales saw a mixed trend in May 2025, with total sales down 0.9 per cent MoM but up 3.3 per cent YoY to $715.4 billion. * Core retail sales remained resilient, rising 4.6 per cent YoY. Retail sales in the United States posted a mixed performance in May 2025, with headline figures declining but core categories showing resilience, according to advance estimates from the US Census Bureau. The total retail and food services sales fell by 0.9 per cent from April, reaching $715.4 billion. Core retail sales—which exclude vehicles, fuel, and restaurants—slipped just 0.1 per cent month-on-month (MoM) but surged 4.6 per cent YoY, underscoring firm consumer spending despite economic headwinds. Non-store retail, led by e-commerce, was a standout performer, rising 0.9 per cent from April and 8.3 per cent from May 2024. US retail sales saw a mixed trend in May 2025, with total sales down 0.9 per cent MoM but up 3.3 per cent YoY to $715.4 billion. Core retail sales remained resilient, rising 4.6 per cent YoY. Inventories stood at $2,656.5 billion, nearly flat MoM but up 2.2 per cent from April 2024, resulting in an improved inventories-to-sales ratio of 1.38, down from 1.4 a year ago. May core retail sales were up 0.1 per cent MoM and 3.9 per cent unadjusted YoY. A 3-month moving average showed a 4.4 per cent annual increase, affirming steady retail momentum, according to the National Retail Federation (NRF) based on the census data. “We are continuing to see growth for core retail sales this year at about the same pace as last year. Retail sales rose 0.9 percent in April as a rebound in automobile sales and a pickup in dining powered another monthly increase in consumer spending, according to data released Tuesday by the Census Bureau. Sales by retailers, restaurants and bars totaled $677.7 billion in April, according to the Census Bureau, up from a revised March total of $671.6 billion. Economists expected retail sales to rise 1 percent last month after auto dealers reported a sharp pickup in sales and restaurant activity rose in April. Both were key drivers of the April increase in retail sales, which has steamed ahead despite inflation hitting an annual rate of 8.3 percent last month, according to Labor Department data. Sales by restaurants and bars rose 2 percent in April, in line with a 1.9 percent monthly increase in March. Retail sales minus auto dealers and auto parts shops rose by 0.6 percent in April, and retail sales without the food and beverage industry rose 0.7 percent. "However, strong growth in retail sales figures year on year also reflects steep inflation, as prices have also risen across the board in recent months.". Federal stimulus and the speedy development of COVID-19 vaccines in the U.S. drove a surge in consumer spending that began in early 2021 and has stretched through the first half of this year. Consumer spending has been resilient even in the face of several waves of COVID-19, supply chain snarls and hiring troubles — all of which have fueled higher prices for many goods. While the steady rise of retail sales has helped power a remarkably quick recovery for the U.S. economy, it also pushed inflation toward its highest annual rate in 40 years. The Federal Reserve began in March a series of interest rate hikes meant to cool inflation by slowing down the U.S. economy. Every one of those dollars moved through a warehouse. And the warehouses winning the volume are the ones running modern management systems. If your operation still tracks inventory on spreadsheets or a legacy platform from 2014, you are not competing. You are waiting to lose a contract. The warehouse management systems market is accelerating, and retail is eating most of the investment. A new market analysis from openPR confirms what operators already feel on the ground: e commerce fulfillment is the primary driver of WMS capital expenditure, not traditional industrial distribution. The retailers and their 3PL partners are building a technology infrastructure that will become the baseline expectation for every distribution contract in the next 18 months. If you run a distribution center, a 3PL operation, or a manufacturing facility with direct to customer shipping, the question is no longer whether to invest. It is whether you can afford the timeline you are on. They accelerated through the back half of 2025 and into 2026, jumping from $731 billion in October 2025 to $752 billion by March 2026. That is $21 billion in incremental monthly volume in five months. Federal Reserve data shows retail sales climbing from $687 billion in April 2024 to $752 billion in March 2026. WMS adoption is the mechanism operators are using to extract more throughput from the same footprint. If the gap is more than 8 to 12 percent, you are already on borrowed time. If you are within range, a WMS implementation locks in that position before the next wave of volume hits. The retail sales surge from $711 billion in January 2025 to $752 billion in March 2026 represents volume that operators had to handle with roughly the same labor pool. Retail sales surging past $739 billion in February 2026 and hitting $752 billion in March tell you that consumer demand is not slowing.

results.content: Title: Christmas retail sales predicted to hit $54.3 billion - Retail Beauty Home » Christmas retail sales predicted to hit $54.3 billion. # Christmas retail sales predicted to hit $54.3 billion. The eagerly anticipated annual Christmas retail sales forecast from the **Australian Retailers Association (ARA)** and **Roy Morgan Research** predicts a 2.8 per cent rise to $54.3 billion – up from $52.9 billion in 2019. There are winners and losers across the six major categories. The most deeply affected areas following this year’s Covid-19 lockdowns are: Hospitality (-18.7% to $6.09 billion) and Clothing, Footwear and Accessories (- 12.2% to $3.71 billion). NSW and Victoria have suffered more than other states during the coronavirus crisis and will not be bolstered by the usual influx of international tourists over the Festive Season this year. But NSW is forecast to remain the number one state market with $16.64 billion – down 0.7 per cent from 2019. Victoria is expected to slide 3.3 percent by contrast to last year to $13.37 billion. File Photo by John Angelillo/UPI. Aug. 15 (UPI) -- The U.S. Census Bureau reported Thursday that July retail sales were better than expected, as consumer inflation also dipped. Retail sales rose 1% over June to $709.7 billion, up 2.7% from a year ago. The increase greatly exceeded Dow Jones economists' expectations of a 0.3% bump. Census data showed total retail and food services sales rose 2.9% over the past seven months. "Retail trade sales were up 1.1% from June 2024, and up 2.6% from last year," the Census Bureau statement said. "Nonstore retailers were up 6.7% from last year, while food services and drinking places were up 3.4% from July 2023.". The Census Bureau found that motor vehicle and parts sales were up 3.6% from a year ago. Electronics and appliance store sales rose 1.6% while retail and food services was up by 1%. "Once again, this was further evidence that the U.S. consumer still has the ability to surprise to the upside," wrote William Blair analyst Richard de Chazal. "This was another solid report, and inconsistent with a consumer who is on the brink of collapse.". The better-than-expected retail sales news came as CPI inflation dropped below 3% for the first time, with year-to-year inflation rising at the slowest rate since March 2021. results.content: Title: Census Bureau: Retail sales show healthy March growth | Chain Store Age Census Bureau: Retail sales show healthy March growth. Retail sales increased in March 2024. Data released by the U.S. Census Bureau shows retail sales continued to increase in March. Core retail sales (excludes automobile dealers, gasoline stations and restaurants) rose 1.1% in March and were up 3.2% year-over-year, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Overall retail in March were up 0.7% from February 2024 and up 4% year-over-year. That compares with increases of 0.9% month-over-month and 2.1% year-over-year. National Retail Federation (NRF) chief economist Jack Kleinhenz said contributors including tax refunds and job growth helped put more money in shoppers’ pockets during the month. "March’s Census Bureau numbers confirm that consumer spending remains steady, underscoring a resilient consumer despite inflationary pressure," Kleinhenz said. "While sales were mixed, several factors supported retail sales including an early Easter holiday, slightly larger 2023 tax refunds and stronger payroll growth over the last three months. Nonetheless, the increasing share of consumer spending going to services as prices for services rise remains a stubborn problem because it leaves less household income available to spend on retail goods.". Core retail sales were up 3.9% unadjusted YoY on a three-month moving average as of March. According to the CNBC/National Retail Federation (NRF) Retail Monitor, total retail sales, excluding automobiles and gasoline, were up 0.36% seasonally adjusted month-over-month and up 2.72% unadjusted year-over-year in March. That compared with increases of 0.4% month-over-month and 2.7% year-over-year in February. The Retail Monitor calculation of core retail sales – excluding restaurants in addition to automobiles and gasoline – was up 0.23% month-over-month and up 2.92% year-over-year in March. Those figures are down slightly compared with increases of 0.27% month-over-month and 2.99% year-over-year in February. For the first quarter, Retail Monitor data indicates total retail sales were up 2.65% year-over-year, while core sales were up 3.12%. In addition, according to Mastercard SpendingPulse, which measures in-store and online retail sales across all forms of payment, total U.S. retail sales (excluding automotive) were up year-over-year in March 2024, showing showing continued growth for both online (+6.1%) and in-store (+2.6%) retail sales. * Research Topic > Consumer Attitudes & Behavior. * Research Topic > Budgets/Spending/Market Size.

results.content: U.S. flag An official website of the United States government Check out our new Automotive Statistics webpage where you can explore, interact with, and discover insights through a wide range of automotive-related indicator data! end of header Census.gov > Business and Economy > Retail - Monthly > About the Surveys > About the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey Skip to looking for section [...] The Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS) provides an early indication of sales of retail and food service companies. It was developed in response to requests by government, business, and other users to provide an early indication of current retail trade activity in the United States. Retail sales are one of the primary measures of consumer demand for both durable and non-durable goods. MARTS also provides an estimate of monthly sales at food service establishments and drinking places. [...] ### Uses This economic indicator is widely used and closely watched throughout government, academic, and business communities. The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses the estimates as an input for estimating Gross Domestic Product. The Federal Reserve Board uses the estimates to anticipate economic trends. The Council of Economic Advisors uses the estimates for economic policy analysis.

results.title: Retail Sales Rose in January
results.content: Title: Retail Sales Rose in January Retail Sales Rose in January. Retail Sales Rose in January Retail Sales Rose in January. Washington, DC, February 12, 2016—Advance estimates of U.S. retail and food services sales for January were $449.9 billion, an increase of 0.2% from the previous month, and 3.4% above January 2015, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Total sales for the November 2015 through January 2016 period were up 2.5% from the same period a year ago. The November 2015 to December 2015 percent change was revised from down 0.1% to up 0.2%. Retail trade sales were up 0.3% from December 2015, and up 3.1% from last year. results.content: The retail sales report, formally the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services, is published by the US Census Bureau, part of the Department of Commerce. It is the first official estimate of how much American consumers spent at retailers and restaurants in the previous month, which is why it is widely known as the “advance” estimate. Markets treat it as one of the principal federal economic indicators, alongside the jobs report and the inflation releases. [...] Because the advance estimate is built from a subsample with a short collection window, it is revised twice: a preliminary revision in the following month’s release and a second revision the month after, when the full survey panel has responded. Revisions can be material. The February 2026 reading, first reported as a 0.6% rise, was later revised up to 0.7%. Annual benchmark revisions, tied to the Annual Retail Trade Survey and the five-yearly Economic Census, can reshape the levels further. results.title: Monthly Retail Trade - About the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey
results.content: Advance sales estimates for each kind of business are developed by applying a ratio of current-month to previous-month sales (derived from the advance retail and food service sample) to the preliminary estimate of sales for the previous month (from the larger monthly sample). results.content: Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau delivers a detailed report on the economic health of consumers, as measured by sales of goods and services at the retail level. It's a key gauge—used by government policymakers, Wall Street analysts, and everyday investors—of how and where we all spent our money the month before. Because consumer spending represents some 70% of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), the results are considered a harbinger of what might be ahead on the economic front. [...] ## The bottom line The monthly retail sales report offers deep and timely insight into how the economy is functioning. Tracking those numbers and the rise and fall in each category over short and long periods provides key metrics that help the government, the Federal Reserve, businesses, and consumers forecast how the economy will move forward and how to prepare accordingly. Specific companies and funds are mentioned in this article for educational purposes only and not as an endorsement. [...] ## Key Points The U.S. Census Bureau collects data each month from retailers across the economy and releases it around the middle of the following month. Retail sales data is used by the Federal Reserve and several government agencies to help inform their policy decisions. Everyday investors can use retail sales data to gauge the strength of the economy and perhaps future employment trends.

results.content: Seth Kerstein Today the U.S. Census Bureau released preliminary estimates of nationwide retail sales in September 2024 and revised estimates for August 2024. (The data include both brick-and-mortar and Internet sales.) Retail Sales Growing. Seasonally adjusted U.S. retail sales grew 1.7 percent from June to September. So if prices are going higher - and they are - retail sales goes higher. **What does the Retail Sales report measure?**. The Advance Monthly Retail Sales report, published by the U.S. Census Bureau, provides the earliest monthly snapshot of consumer spending across retail sectors. Released approximately two weeks after the end of each reference month at 8:30 a.m. ET, the report measures sales at retail and food service establishments, adjusted for seasonal variation and holiday and trading-day differences but not for price changes. The data serves as a critical indicator of consumer demand and economic health, tracking thirteen major retail categories from motor vehicles and electronics to food services and nonstore retailers. The report includes both headline retail sales and "retail control" sales, which exclude more volatile categories like autos, gasoline, and building materials, providing a cleaner measure of underlying consumer spending that feeds into GDP calculations.
